systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : Politico Europe
Rubrique : Europe
Date du flux : 19/11/2026
Auteur : Max Griera; Carlo Martuscelli
Titre d'origine : EU lawmakers accuse Chinese officials of intimidation over Taiwan

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (Politico Europe) :
BRUSSELS — EU lawmakers from across the political spectrum say they have come under pressure from the Chinese government for traveling to or communicating with Taiwan.
Eight MEPs gave accounts of what some described as intimidation inside the European Parliament — including a senior Chinese diplomat turning up unannounced at one MEP’s office — detentions at the Chinese border and threatening letters.
The incidents come a little over a year after the European Parliament and Beijing restored ties following years of fraught relations over European criticism of China’s treatment of ethnic and religious minorities, and against the backdrop of European manufacturers creaking under the competitive pressure of Chinese imports.

SOURCE 2 (Mezha.net) :
EU lawmakers say China pressured them over Taiwan ties
Photo source: Politico
Several MEPs say Chinese officials sought to deter their travel to or communications with Taiwan. Parliament President Roberta Metsola is in contact with Chinese authorities over the reported incidents.
Eight EU lawmakers from across the political spectrum described pressure they say they faced from the Chinese government. Their accounts included a senior Chinese diplomat’s unannounced visit to an MEP’s office, a lawmaker being detained at the Chinese border and letters urging MEPs to avoid official contact with Taiwan.
This is reported by Politico.
The accounts come a little over a year after the European Parliament and Beijing restored ties following years of strained relations over European criticism of China’s treatment of ethnic and religious minorities. Taiwan has been politically separate from China since 1949. Beijing claims the island, home to 23 million people, as part of its territory; the EU and its member countries do not recognize Taiwan as a separate country.
Engin Eroglu, a German liberal MEP who chairs the Parliament’s delegation to China, said he had received “fierce” pushback from Beijing but did not specify what it involved. “I have never encountered such behavior from foreign diplomats,” he said. The Chinese mission to the EU did not reply to requests for comment.
Before a June 2025 visit to Taiwan, António Tânger Corrêa, vice-chair of the far-right Patriots group, said a senior Chinese diplomat came to his office unannounced and warned that they “could not ensure” his safety and “didn’t know what could happen” if he travelled. Corrêa said Metsola offered to warn the Chinese mission or take tougher action, but he urged her to pursue diplomacy first.
MEPs who attended a forum in Taipei in October 2026 received letters, seen by POLITICO, from China’s EU mission urging them to “refrain from any official exchange in whatever form with the Taiwan authorities.” Czech MEP Ondřej Krutílek, who received a letter, said: “China has no right to intimidate elected representatives or interfere with their parliamentary work.” Other recipients included Michal Kobosko, Rihard Kols, Bernard Guetta and Michael Gahler.
Kobosko called the letter “bizarre” and said, “We cannot accept acts of direct pressure against us.” Guetta said meetings with China were usually “completely polite,” but the letter was sent “to try pressure.” Kols described its tone as “quite aggressive,” while saying he did not see it as grounds to tighten access rules for Chinese officials or ask Metsola to intervene.
Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Green MEP and vice-chair of the Parliament’s China delegation, said Chinese officials stopped her at Beijing border control on Sept. 26, confiscated her passport and barred her from using her phone. She said she was surrounded by police and held for about an hour and a half. “It was an extremely unpleasant experience and, without my colleagues there to help me, it would have been frightening,” she told POLITICO.
Gregorová is leading the revision of the Cybersecurity Act, a proposal that could exclude Chinese telecom suppliers from European networks. Chinese officials have threatened “countermeasures” if it passes. Gregorová said she did not know whether the border incident was an administrative error or a “deliberate intimidation tactic.” She said she was sending a letter to China’s National People’s Congress demanding an explanation and would ask Metsola to bar Chinese representatives from Parliament unless one was provided.
Metsola has been in close contact with the MEPs concerned and “has conveyed our questions and concerns directly to the Chinese authorities,” her spokesperson, Juri Laas, said. “Diplomatic contacts are ongoing in an effort to ensure that further incidents can be avoided.” Laas added that MEPs should be able to exercise their freedom of mandate and that members travelling with an official Parliament delegation should not have problems entering their host country.
Earlier in 2026, POLITICO reported that Chinese officials had told MEPs in the Socialists and Democrats group not to vote for a report critical of Beijing, warning of possible consequences. In 2021, Beijing sanctioned five MEPs after EU sanctions targeting alleged abuses of Uyghur rights. The Parliament responded by freezing ratification of an EU-China investment deal and halting diplomatic contact with Beijing.
